claim: Phase v27 implemented the user-proposed strategy: train motif scanners (PWMs) on Salmonella LT2's RegulonDB-enriched GenBank annotation (the only one of our 16 GenBanks with /regulatory and /protein_bind features — 3965 ribosome binding sites, 256 minus_10 signals, 256 minus_35 signals, 397 protein-binding sites covering 14 major TFs), then apply those PWMs to score upstream regions in all 16 organisms uniformly to predict regulatory features that aren't explicitly labeled. Result: cross-organism MCC on Syn3A DROPPED from v25's 0.2268 (original 20 features) to 0.1069 (original 20 + 50 predicted regulatory features) — delta -0.1199. PWMs trained on Salmonella's labels DID validate well on Salmonella SELF for the RBS class (precision=0.848, recall=0.804) but showed near-zero precision on the other regulatory classes (-10 signal P=0.066, -35 signal P=0.062, most TFs P=0.001-0.020) because the underlying motifs are short (6-9bp) and abundant by chance in any 200bp upstream window. Cross-organism application failed worse: the predicted regulatory features for non-Salmonella organisms are largely noise because regulatory grammar is organism-specific (Mycoplasma's GC=30% sequences score the Salmonella GC=52%-trained PWMs differently than Mycoplasma's actual regulatory elements would). Top-15 feature importances from the augmented GB confirm: the original features (gc, is_putative, kw_translation, is_hypothetical, kw_synthase, operon_run_length, position_norm, log_length_bp, kw_replication) dominate with importances 0.03-0.25; regulatory features rank 10-15 with importances 0.007-0.012, contributing more noise than signal. The user-proposed strategy is biologically motivated but bottlenecked by motif-grammar specificity to organism background composition; PWMs trained on one bacterium do not generalize to phylogenetically distant ones.
source_detail: Reproducible via scripts/predict_regulatory_features.py (extracts Salmonella's labeled regulatory positions, builds PWMs via Bio.motifs from labeled sequences, scans 200bp upstream of every CDS in all 16 GenBanks for each PWM, calibrates per-PWM threshold at 80% recall on Salmonella self) and scripts/train_with_regulatory_features.py (4 GB+LogReg variants on the augmented features). Outputs: outputs/multiorg_per_gene_features_with_regulatory.csv, outputs/regulatory_motif_validation.json, outputs/multiorg_classifier_with_regulatory_results.json.
caveats: PWM cross-organism transfer is fundamentally bottlenecked by sequence-background composition. Salmonella has 52% GC content; Mycoplasma has 30%. PWMs trained on Salmonella are scored against Mycoplasma backgrounds via log-odds vs uniform — but the actual background frequencies differ. Even if Mycoplasma RBSes follow the same Shine-Dalgarno consensus, the score distributions look different because the random-background expected frequency is different.

Even Salmonella's own PWM precision is poor for short motifs. The -10 box (TATAAT) and -35 box (TTGACA) are 6 bp; in a 200bp upstream window there are ~190 possible positions, so chance hits are abundant. Per-PWM precision on Salmonella's own labeled positions: -10 = 0.066, -35 = 0.062. The labeled positions ARE detected (recall ~0.8) but so are 14× as many false positives. For cross-organism prediction this means: the predicted promoter features are mostly noise.

The RBS PWM (P=0.85, R=0.80 on Salmonella self) is the only motif that generalizes well numerically, but biology cuts both ways: Mycoplasma RBSes are weaker / shorter than enterobacterial ones (well-documented in the literature — Mycoplasma uses an alternative AUG-context recognition mechanism with degraded Shine-Dalgarno), so Salmonella's RBS PWM systematically under-detects them. v27's confusion-matrix shift (TP up by +131 from 235 to 366, FP up by +42, TN down by -42 from 50 to 8) shows the model is now MORE eager to call essential — the RBS feature pushes prediction up but doesn't carry organism-discriminative signal.

What WOULD have worked: per-organism PWM training. Build Salmonella PWMs from Salmonella labels, apply only to Salmonella; build Mycoplasma PWMs from observable Mycoplasma sequence patterns near start codons (anti-Shine-Dalgarno region of 16S rRNA tells you the species-specific RBS consensus). This was not done because it requires per-organism analysis pipelines outside the current scope.

What COULD still help: download and integrate RegulonDB (E. coli K-12) and SubtiWiki (B. subtilis 168) curated regulatory data. We have GenBanks for both organisms but no essentiality (Goodall 2018 ecoli + Koo 2017 bsubtilis are MISSING in the data acquisition per the supp MANIFEST.tsv). With RegulonDB+Keio for E. coli (hypothetical Phase 7), we'd have 2 organisms with rich regulatory annotation as training data; cross-organism transfer should improve.

User's strategic intent was correct: use organism with rich regulatory labels to bootstrap predictions for organisms without labels. The execution requires either (a) per-organism PWM calibration, (b) species-specific motif models, or (c) a deep neural network that learns organism-conditioned motif representations. Naive PWM transfer with a single Salmonella-trained model fails because regulatory grammar varies across phylogenetic distance.

Confidence: measured (the experiment is reproducible, the validation on Salmonella self is well-defined, the cross-organism MCC drop is robustly negative across all model variants tried). The v25 GB at 0.2268 remains the best cross-organism Syn3A predictor on this 14k-gene multi-bacterial dataset; v27's predicted regulatory features added noise rather than signal.
